title: Singer-Songwriter / Folk
text:
Singer-Songwriter / Folk
Lessons in this direction may involve open chords, strumming, fingerpicking, rhythm, chord changes, capo use, chord embellishments, and playing while singing.
The guitar doesn’t always need to be the center of attention. A big part of this kind of playing is learning how to support a song and make rhythm, dynamics, and chord choices work with everything else that’s happening.
We can use songs you already enjoy to study different accompaniment styles and gradually build a larger collection of patterns and ideas you can use elsewhere.
This path is a starting point, not a fixed curriculum.

title: Rock / Alternative
text:
Rock / Alternative
Lessons in rock and alternative may involve riffs, power chords, rhythm playing, muting, picking technique, lead playing, alternate tunings, and learning parts directly from recordings.
A lot of the direction will depend on the bands and guitarists you listen to. Songs can give us a reason to work on certain techniques rather than learning them as isolated exercises.
As you get more comfortable, we can also pay closer attention to the smaller things that give different players their sound, like timing, dynamics, articulation, pick attack, and the way riffs or chords are actually played.
This path is a starting point, not a fixed curriculum.

title: About Me
text:
I know what it’s like to learn guitar without having one perfectly organized path laid out in front of you. It can be frustrating and tedious, but I also think some amount of struggling, experimenting, and figuring things out for yourself is an important part of becoming a musician.


And occasionally it might make you look like this.

I want lessons to give students structure without taking away that curiosity.
Rather than simply being told “play this scale 100 times,” I want students to eventually start asking:

Why does that sound like that?


Why does this player phrase it that way?


How can I make it sound like me?

That’s the kind of musician I want to help someone become.




I grew up in Tulare, a small city in California’s Central Valley. For the past three years, Isla Vista has been home while I’ve been working toward a Physics B.S. at UCSB. Music wasn’t a particularly strong part of my family or the scene I grew up around, so I feel fortunate that I eventually stumbled onto a guitar on my own.
The first time I held one was about two weeks after hearing Nirvana’s MTV Unplugged performance of The Man Who Sold the World. I had played some trumpet in middle school, but otherwise had very little musical experience. Trying to learn the song through tabs and YouTube tutorials left me feeling like I was copying instructions without really understanding what I was hearing.
A physics teacher of mine gave me a piece of advice that changed the way I learned: ditch the tutorials and tabs for a while, use your ear, and try to find the notes on the guitar by singing them first.
That sent me in a completely different direction. I began learning more and more directly from recordings, slowing songs down, replaying small sections, and searching for the sounds on the fretboard myself. Tabs and tutorials are great tools, especially when the goal is simply to learn a song quickly, but I found that I wanted to dig further into the instrument.
Guitar also changed the way I listened to music. Wanting new things to play pushed me toward genres and artists I probably never would have discovered otherwise. I started spending long stretches studying albums: slowing passages down, noticing small details in a player’s rhythm or technique, learning some of the theory behind what I heard, and collecting those little musical ideas into my own growing mixture of influences.
That process eventually changed the way I listen to music in general. I became less interested in simply learning the notes of a song and more interested in understanding why different players sound like themselves.
That’s a big reason I wanted to start teaching.
I want to help other players develop the same tools that made guitar exciting for me: listening closely, experimenting, developing an ear, understanding the instrument, and eventually building a musical voice of their own.

title: Lead Guitar
text:
Lead Guitar
Lead guitar lessons may involve bends, vibrato, phrasing, timing, articulation, picking, fretboard navigation, improvisation, and learning solos or smaller phrases directly from recordings.
Knowing which notes to play is only half of the story. We can spend time looking at how different guitarists actually produce those notes and what makes their playing recognizable.
Over time, learning ideas from several different players can help you add licks to your back pocket to experiment with and eventually combine in your own way.
This path is a starting point, not a fixed curriculum.
Book a First Lesson

title: Absolute Beginner
text:
Absolute Beginner
Lessons for beginners may involve tuning, basic rhythm, chords, riffs, picking, fretboard fundamentals, and beginning to learn simple tunes by ear.
If you’ve never played before, that’s completely fine. Early lessons would mostly be about getting comfortable with the instrument and figuring out what kinds of music you actually want to play.
The plan won’t be to bombard you with a giant list of guitar concepts before you’re allowed to have fun with the instrument. I’ll establish the fundamentals while figuring out what kind of player you aim to be, and we’ll gradually start using songs and recordings as part of the learning process.
This path is a starting point, not a fixed curriculum.
Book a First Lesson

title: My Approach
text:
My Approach
Based on a student’s experience and interests, the order in which we learn things will vary. A fan of metal or rock may start with power chords early on, while someone completely new may first need to learn how to properly tune and handle their guitar. Over time, I want students to gain intuition and become comfortable learning from recordings rather than depending entirely on tabs or someone else giving them the answers.
A central part of that is learning to listen beyond the notes themselves. Guitar has an enormous number of subtle variables that can completely change the sound of a phrase even when the pitch stays the same. Miles Davis was an artist deeply concerned with shaping deliberate sounds, and I think that same attention can be applied to guitar. Right-hand position, pick angle, pick velocity, muting, dynamics, timing, bends, vibrato, and even the space between notes can all contribute to a player’s personality. If we’re studying somebody else’s playing, finding the correct frets and notes shouldn’t be the end goal. We should try to understand the details that created the sound we heard, learn to reproduce them ourselves, and add those ideas to our own musical vocabulary.
I also don’t see imitation as the opposite of developing your own style. Studying several musicians closely gives you more vocabulary to work with. You might absorb one player’s rhythm, another player’s vibrato, a chord voicing from somewhere else, and a handful of licks or phrasing ideas from completely different styles. Eventually those influences begin colliding and combining in ways that none of the original players necessarily would have used themselves. To me, that’s part of the process of building a unique musical identity.

title: Blues
text:
Blues
Blues lessons may involve rhythm, pentatonic ideas, bends, vibrato, phrasing, improvisation, chord progressions, and learning licks or solos by ear.
The blues is especially useful for learning how much can be done with a relatively small amount of musical material. Two players can use almost the same pentatonic box and still sound completely different.
Because of that, a lot of attention can go toward timing, touch, bends, vibrato, dynamics, and the space between notes rather than simply memorizing scale shapes.
This path is a starting point, not a fixed curriculum.
Book a First Lesson

title: Jazz Foundations
text:
Jazz Foundations
Jazz lessons at this level would focus on building a foundation in the harmony, rhythm, and vocabulary used in jazz guitar.
Depending on your experience, we may look at seventh chords, simple chord voicings, ii-V-I progressions, chord tones, arpeggios, voice leading, basic improvisation, and approachable jazz standards.
The theory will be connected to actual music as much as possible. Recordings can help us hear what the chords and ideas are doing before worrying about giving everything a name.
This path focuses on the foundations of jazz rather than advanced jazz study, and is not a fixed curriculum.
